frictionVectors.title: European gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over upstream hydrocarbons and export infrastructure, but European demand and investment needs create recurring leverage over pricing and supply policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya increases border-security costs and complicates Algeria's effort to preserve strategic autonomy from external military actors.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and Western financing remain important to Angola's infrastructure and mineral-logistics ambitions, limiting room for fully independent project selection and revenue allocation.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The corridor is becoming a major U.S., European, and Chinese strategic arena for copper and cobalt access, giving outside powers influence over Angola's transport and resource priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border and transit rupture
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Niger and wider Sahel instability threaten northern trade routes and complicate Benin's dependence on regional corridors for port revenues and fuel flows.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and port exposure
frictionVectors.details: The oil-export pipeline and port expansion increase national revenue potential but also deepen exposure to foreign operators, lenders, and security guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers partnership tension
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has improved its negotiating position with De Beers, but the diamond sector remains vulnerable to global demand shifts and the commercial influence of a major foreign partner.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral diversification race
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals could reduce diamond dependence, while foreign capital and infrastructure requirements may constrain local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector state control
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking tighter oversight of industrial and artisanal gold, improving the political claim to resource sovereignty while raising concerns about transparency, smuggling, and investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security assistance and continued jihadist violence reduce policy autonomy and expose mining zones, transport routes, and border infrastructure to external and armed-group leverage.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND NICKEL GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Bujumbura is seeking greater state control and formalization of gold and nickel production, but weak oversight and informal extraction limit public revenue. Foreign operators remain important to financing and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: RWANDA SECURITY FRICTION
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain a major sovereignty concern, with accusations of support for armed groups and recurring border restrictions. The dispute complicates trade, security coordination, and regional infrastructure access.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND MARITIME COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is leveraging its Atlantic position for transshipment, maritime security, and digital connectivity, attracting European, Chinese, and other external partners. This creates bargaining opportunities but also dependence on foreign capital and strategic infrastructure operators.

frictionVectors.title: WATER AND ENERGY IMPORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago remains exposed to imported fuel, food, and desalination costs, limiting practical control over core resources. Climate stress and tourism concentration increase vulnerability to external price shocks.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL CONTROL OF EXTRACTIVE CHAINS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and lenders remain central to Cameroon’s oil, gas, mining, timber, and major transport projects. The state captures substantial rents but faces transparency, debt-service, and local-benefit pressures.

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE SECURITY AND INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest continues to threaten roads, plantations, energy assets, and cross-border commerce. Security-first governance constrains local political legitimacy and increases reliance on external security and financing partners.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY-RESOURCE NEXUS
frictionVectors.details: Bangui remains heavily dependent on Russian-linked security support, while access to mining concessions and commercial influence gives Moscow-aligned actors leverage over strategic resources. This narrows the government’s room to diversify partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: ARTISANAL MINING AND ARMED CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Gold and diamond production is concentrated in informal and insecure zones, where armed groups and intermediaries capture value. Limited state presence and weak export controls reduce sovereign revenue and complicate international certification.

frictionVectors.title: OIL DEPENDENCE AND PIPELINE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s fiscal capacity and external bargaining power remain tied to oil production, export infrastructure, and foreign operators. Price volatility, contract asymmetry, and limited domestic refining constrain effective sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN BORDER AND FOREIGN SECURITY TIES
frictionVectors.details: The war in Sudan continues to drive refugee flows, arms trafficking, and militia activity along Chad’s eastern frontier. N’Djamena’s security dependence on external partners and regional alignments complicates independent resource and border policy.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France's administration of Mayotte remains the central sovereignty dispute, constraining Comoros' control over maritime space, migration policy, and regional diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic capital leaves major transport, energy, and telecommunications projects dependent on foreign donors and contractors, reducing national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Armed Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and other armed groups continues to undermine state authority and expose eastern mineral zones to illicit taxation and cross-border influence.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-led investment dominates much of the copper and cobalt value chain, while weak enforcement limits Kinshasa's ability to capture a larger share of downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Concentration
frictionVectors.details: State finances remain heavily exposed to oil prices and foreign operators, leaving limited room to build sovereign control over production, revenues, and refining.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction support roads, ports, and public works, but repayment obligations and opaque contracting can narrow Brazzaville's policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Processing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan is expanding local processing and farmer support, but international buyers and volatile prices still capture substantial value from the country's dominant export.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: French, Chinese, Gulf, and other external investors compete across ports, transport, energy, and digital infrastructure, creating opportunities while complicating strategic alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Presence
frictionVectors.details: Multiple foreign military facilities provide revenue and security but constrain Djibouti's strategic freedom and make the country vulnerable to rivalry around the Red Sea.

frictionVectors.title: Port Debt and Chinese Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed port and rail infrastructure has strengthened connectivity but increased exposure to debt, commercial renegotiation, and external influence over critical logistics assets.

frictionVectors.title: Suez and Red Sea disruption
frictionVectors.details: Houthi attacks and wider Red Sea insecurity continue to divert shipping around the Cape, weakening Egypt's foreign-exchange earnings from the canal. Cairo remains dependent on naval coordination with external partners to protect the route.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF support and Gulf investment are stabilizing Egypt's balance of payments but increase outside influence over privatization, exchange-rate policy, and strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling production is eroding state revenues and increasing pressure to attract foreign operators and regional gas partners. The government retains formal control but has limited bargaining power as reserves mature.

frictionVectors.title: China-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Major public works and financing ties with Chinese firms provide critical infrastructure while deepening dependence on external contractors and creditors. Low transparency complicates assessment of long-term sovereign liabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Regional port competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb give it strategic value amid conflict in Sudan and Yemen. External powers seek access and influence, while Asmara resists arrangements that could constrain its autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and sanctions exposure
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects remain important sources of hard currency but rely on foreign capital, technology, and transport links. Sanctions risk and opaque state involvement limit the country's ability to convert mineral wealth into broad sovereign capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Single-market vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's trade, energy, logistics, and fiscal position remain closely tied to South Africa and the Southern African Customs Union. This provides stability but constrains independent economic and infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and water competition
frictionVectors.details: Sugar exports and irrigation depend on regional markets and shared water systems, exposing the kingdom to climate stress and downstream bargaining pressure. Diversification efforts remain modest.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam has strengthened Ethiopia's control over its electricity and water infrastructure, but operating arrangements remain a persistent source of tension with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and strategic corridors
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages give creditors and partners greater influence over industrial assets, logistics, and telecom expansion. Conflict-related insecurity further raises dependence on external humanitarian and security support.

highlights: State Reasserts Control Over Strategic Minerals

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Manganese and Oil
frictionVectors.details: Gabon is pressing for greater state participation and local processing, but foreign operators still dominate financing, technology, and export logistics. The government must balance resource nationalism against the need to attract capital.

frictionVectors.title: French Commercial Influence
frictionVectors.details: French firms retain important positions in energy, services, and infrastructure despite Libreville's effort to diversify partners. The transition authorities are using Chinese, Gulf, and regional alternatives to increase bargaining power.

highlights: Tourism and Fisheries Anchor a Small Economy
Senegal Remains the Essential Strategic Partner

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fishing and limited monitoring capacity constrain Gambian control over coastal resources. Illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing remains a persistent sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on Senegalese Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Trade routes, electricity links, and access through Senegal provide essential connectivity but limit policy autonomy. Border and transport frictions can quickly affect food, fuel, and export security.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing and Debt Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed stabilization and debt restructuring are constraining fiscal choices while Ghana seeks to preserve control over gold, oil, and critical infrastructure. External creditors retain substantial leverage over economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Influence in Gold Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Illegal mining, environmental damage, and opaque trading networks weaken state control over gold production. Chinese-linked equipment and trading channels remain a prominent concern alongside domestic enforcement failures.

highlights: Simandou Becomes a National Power Project

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Rail and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore complex could transform Guinea but relies on foreign-led financing, construction, and export infrastructure. The state is gaining revenue and leverage, yet remains exposed to partner disputes and commodity-cycle risk.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Dominance and Environmental Stress
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains heavily dependent on externally operated bauxite extraction, with limited domestic processing. Mining expansion is intensifying land, water, and community tensions while deepening reliance on foreign logistics and capital.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capture of Cashew Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Exporters and intermediaries capture much of the value from Guinea-Bissau's dominant cashew sector, leaving the state vulnerable to price shocks and external purchasing power. Limited processing capacity prevents meaningful domestic resource upgrading.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security and Offshore Access
frictionVectors.details: Weak naval and customs capacity leaves coastal fisheries and offshore resources exposed to foreign exploitation. Political instability also creates openings for trafficking networks and complicates cooperation with regional and international security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is renegotiating the balance between Chinese-financed infrastructure, debt-service demands, and domestic control over strategic transport assets. Nairobi is diversifying financing toward Gulf, Western, and multilateral partners.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Energy Investment
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in geothermal power, rare-earth prospects, and other minerals is increasing. Regulatory capacity and revenue-sharing arrangements remain vulnerable to outside pressure and domestic contestation.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Transfers
frictionVectors.details: South Africa remains the dominant buyer and infrastructure partner for Lesotho's water exports, limiting Maseru's bargaining autonomy. Construction delays, compensation disputes, and unequal benefit perceptions continue to generate friction.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Trade and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho relies heavily on South African markets, electricity links, and remittances. This dependence constrains independent resource and industrial policy while exposing the country to Pretoria's regulatory and political leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Large-Scale Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining and infrastructure firms remain central to Liberia's exports and fiscal outlook, but land access, local employment, environmental impacts, and contract transparency remain contentious. The government is seeking greater domestic value capture without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Freeport of Monrovia Strategic Interest
frictionVectors.details: The port is vital to Liberia's trade and attracts competing external commercial and security interests. Modernization offers revenue gains but raises concerns over long-term control of logistics infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Authorities and Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Libya's oil sector remains exposed to rival political and armed networks that can disrupt production, appointments, and revenue distribution. International companies and foreign states retain substantial influence through investment, security ties, and mediation.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, Migration, and External Security Presence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, European states, and regional actors compete for influence over bases, ports, migration routes, and energy corridors. This external security footprint limits unified Libyan control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and ilmenite projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented infrastructure. Madagascar is seeking more processing and fiscal benefit, but weak institutions and infrastructure constrain bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Ports and Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: External partners are competing for influence over ports, telecommunications, energy, and transport corridors across the Indian Ocean. Financing needs make Madagascar receptive to investment while increasing concerns about long-term strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Lithium
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking foreign capital for uranium, rare earths and lithium projects, but limited fiscal capacity weakens its bargaining position over ownership, taxation and local processing.

frictionVectors.title: Import and Power Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Fuel shortages, foreign-exchange scarcity and unreliable electricity expose Malawi to external lenders, import suppliers and infrastructure financiers.

highlights: Junta asserts control over gold sector

frictionVectors.title: Gold Nationalism and Contract Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The government is revising mining rules and pressing foreign operators for greater state participation, increasing tensions with international companies and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support provides regime protection but creates strategic dependence and complicates relations with Western governments and regional institutions.

highlights: Gas exports enter a strategic phase

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major revenue and infrastructure opportunities, while cross-border governance and revenue management remain sensitive sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Extractive Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, ports and prospective green-hydrogen projects depend heavily on foreign operators and capital, limiting near-term domestic control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Settlement Implementation
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to the future of the Diego Garcia military facility and requires careful management of relations with the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence in Energy and Food
frictionVectors.details: As a small island economy, Mauritius remains exposed to imported fuel, food and maritime-disruption risks despite progress in renewables and higher-value services.

highlights: Western Sahara remains central to diplomacy

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Recognition Contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate resources, infrastructure and diplomatic partnerships to consolidate control, while recognition disputes continue to shape relations with Algeria, the EU and African partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, Gulf and other investors support ports, renewables, automobiles and logistics, creating growth while raising questions about dependency and strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International energy firms and lenders retain major leverage over Mozambique's offshore gas development, revenue structures, and project timelines. A restart of large-scale LNG activity could strengthen state finances but deepen dependence on external capital and security guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgency and External Security Support
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence in Cabo Delgado continues to constrain sovereign control over gas-producing territory. Regional and foreign military assistance remains important, exposing Maputo to outside influence over security priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Ownership Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Recent oil discoveries have increased competition among international energy companies for offshore concessions. Namibia is seeking greater local participation and fiscal returns while avoiding overdependence on foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Infrastructure Financing
frictionVectors.details: Green hydrogen, port, and transmission projects require substantial external finance and technology. Chinese, European, and Gulf-linked capital could expand infrastructure but create competing strategic dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Reorientation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is renegotiating its relationship with Western mining interests while seeking alternatives through Russian and other non-Western partnerships. This increases bargaining leverage but risks reduced investment, sanctions exposure, and operational disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Pipeline Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Niger's crude exports depend heavily on cross-border infrastructure and stable relations with coastal transit states. Political isolation, insecurity, and disputes over revenue-sharing continue to limit effective sovereign control of export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria needs international finance and technical partners to restore upstream production, yet contract uncertainty, theft, and regulatory disputes weaken state leverage. The government is attempting to capture more value through revised fiscal terms and domestic content requirements.

frictionVectors.title: Refining and Pipeline Security
frictionVectors.details: The Dangote refinery and planned domestic refining capacity could reduce dependence on imported fuel and external supply chains. Persistent pipeline vandalism, crude theft, and infrastructure bottlenecks continue to undermine energy sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict Minerals and DRC Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role in regional mineral trade remains under intense scrutiny, particularly over alleged links between eastern DRC conflict networks and mineral exports. Diplomatic and economic pressure from the DRC and international partners threatens Kigali's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Strategic Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's development model relies on foreign aid, investment, and security partnerships while emphasizing domestic control and state-led coordination. Donor criticism over regional military activity could translate into conditionality or reduced financial support.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Licensing
frictionVectors.details: Unproven offshore petroleum prospects attract foreign energy firms, but limited state capacity and uncertain commercial discoveries constrain São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, connectivity, and tourism projects rely heavily on external finance, creating exposure to competing Portuguese, Chinese, and other international interests.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater domestic value capture and transparency in offshore projects, creating friction with international operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Fishing Access Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial and foreign fishing interests compete with Senegalese small-scale fleets, while enforcement and stock depletion remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing and Maritime Access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from licensing and maritime partnerships but must balance foreign fishing activity against conservation, local control, and sovereign surveillance.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Indian, European, and other partners support maritime security and infrastructure, giving Victoria useful leverage while increasing sensitivity around strategic access.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Rutile Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-controlled mining remains central to export earnings, leaving Sierra Leone exposed to commodity cycles and disputes over taxation, land, and domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Resources Risk
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external firms provide capital and construction capacity, but opaque terms and limited local procurement can weaken long-term sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil and Licensing Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Prospective petroleum development is entangled with federal-regional authority disputes and foreign operator interests, limiting Somalia's ability to establish unified resource governance.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security and Port Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Gulf, Western, and regional security partnerships support state capacity but also generate competing influence around ports, logistics, fisheries, and maritime access.

highlights: Power and port bottlenecks constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Critical minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Competition among the United States, China, and Gulf investors for platinum-group metals, manganese, and battery minerals tests Pretoria's ability to secure domestic beneficiation.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and logistics decay
frictionVectors.details: Persistent grid weakness and rail-port congestion reduce export control and industrial leverage, while external capital becomes increasingly important for infrastructure recovery.

highlights: Oil dependence limits sovereign bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on Sudanese export infrastructure, leaving petroleum revenue exposed to conflict, pipeline disruptions, and Khartoum-linked bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign security and aid footprint
frictionVectors.details: Regional mediation, humanitarian operations, and external security relationships remain essential as weak institutions limit state control over land, oil, and transport corridors.

highlights: War fragments control of strategic assets
Red Sea access attracts outside competition

frictionVectors.title: Gold and wartime supply chains
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed actors and foreign-linked commercial networks capture value from gold and other commodities, weakening centralized resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor geopolitics
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and Nile-facing transport routes is strategically contested, with Gulf, Egyptian, Russian, and regional interests shaping infrastructure access.

highlights: Mining and gas bargaining is tightening

frictionVectors.title: Resource-contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater state participation and local value addition in gold, graphite, nickel, and natural gas, creating friction with multinational investors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail competition
frictionVectors.details: The Dar es Salaam corridor and planned rail links draw competing Gulf, Chinese, and Western interest, raising concerns over long-term control of strategic infrastructure.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional logistics hub

frictionVectors.title: Port influence and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's importance as a maritime and transshipment hub attracts external financing and commercial influence, creating ongoing questions about strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence and political instability moving south from Burkina Faso threaten northern transport corridors and may increase reliance on foreign security assistance.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains dependent on European financing and cooperation while resisting direct European involvement in border enforcement. Migration agreements risk converting fiscal and security needs into external policy leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Italy and European partners are expanding influence through gas, electricity, and renewable-energy links. These projects may improve supply but could limit Tunisia's policy autonomy if domestic financing remains weak.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP External Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Uganda retains strong formal control over its oil resources, but the Tanzania pipeline is exposed to financing, environmental, and political pressure from Western actors. Delays would increase dependence on foreign contractors and state-backed lenders.

frictionVectors.title: China-West Competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese infrastructure and security cooperation remain important, while Western governments retain influence through aid, trade, and governance pressure. Kampala is balancing partners to preserve room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt are drawing intensified interest from China, the United States, the European Union, and Gulf investors. Zambia's push for local processing faces pressure from foreign capital seeking preferential access to raw materials.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Transport Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and constrained rail corridors limit Zambia's ability to capture more value from mining. Dependence on regional infrastructure and emergency power imports weakens bargaining leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Gold Access
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain prominent in lithium and other mineral projects, while Western and regional investors seek greater access to strategic resources. Weak transparency and limited domestic processing reduce Zimbabwe's ability to retain value.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, sanctions-related constraints, and unreliable electricity increase reliance on external financiers and neighboring power systems. These pressures constrain the state's capacity to regulate extractive projects on its own terms.
